intro: glTF to STL converts 3D models from glTF to STL on the server, with nothing to install. It is useful, for example, to print a glTF model exported from an editor or a game engine. STL is the format every slicer reads (PrusaSlicer, Cura, Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer): it only stores triangles, with no units or colours.

glTF is Khronos' open 3D format for the web and apps; a .gltf is a JSON file that can carry its data embedded or in separate .bin files. As glTF uses the Y axis up and 3D printing uses Z, the model is turned so it stands upright in the slicer; if you do not want that, tick “Keep the original axes” in the advanced options. The .gltf must carry its data embedded: if it uses a separate .bin, upload it as GLB, which puts everything in one file.

You can apply a scale, choose the original's units if the glTF does not store them and decide what to do with the parts: keep them separate inside the STL when the format allows it, merge them into one mesh or get one file per part in a ZIP.

The glTF geometry reaches the STL without being simplified or repaired. Up to one million triangles are accepted without an account, two million with a free account and ten million with Pro, and up to ten files per task; they are processed on our server in the European Union and deleted when they expire.
steps: Upload one or more glTF files.
Choose the units and, optionally, the scale and parts.

faq.q: Why does the STL come out rotated or on its side?
faq.a: Because glTF and STL may use different axes. Try ticking or unticking “Keep the original axes” in the advanced options.
The glTF material colours go into the STL if the format supports them; STL stores no colours and the note says so.

faq.q: What if the model has holes?
faq.a: The STL has the same geometry as the glTF. To close them before printing, use Repair STL.
